name: tagless-final
intent: Abstract a program over the interpretation of its effects by expressing the domain's operations as an algebra - a type class, interface or dictionary of callables - whose result type is an opaque interpretation type, so that one program text is interpreted by many interpreters (evaluator, pretty-printer, compiler, test double) without ever building a tagged syntax tree.
problem: Domain logic is entangled with the concrete effect it runs in and with one representation of its operations, so the logic can only be executed one way: it cannot be printed, analysed, compiled to another target or tested without the real effect, and swapping a dependency (Future for IO, database for in-memory store) means editing every place that names it.
context: Statically typed functional or hybrid codebases (Scala, Haskell/OCaml, TypeScript with fp-ts, C# with LanguageExt, C++ template code) where a domain's operations must be interpreted in several ways - production effect, test double, printer, code generator - and the effect type constructor itself (F[_] over IO, Task, Either, ZIO) must stay out of the domain logic. Typically an application core in a hexagonal or clean architecture, or the front end of a compiler whose later stages are interpretations of one algebra.
benefits: One program text, many meanings: evaluate, pretty-print, compile, analyse or mock the same expression without touching it, because the program is written against the algebra, not against an interpreter.
New interpreters are free and non-breaking - the open side of the expression problem - and new syntax is added by composing additional algebras behind extra constraints.

Type safety without tags: the host type checker guarantees that every interpreter handles every construct it was written for; there is no tag to mismatch at run time, and the interpreters cannot get stuck.

No intermediate data structure is materialised, so the interpreted values are produced directly by natural recursion over the program - a performance and allocation win over an AST plus a separate pass.
The effect is a boundary decision: the same logic runs over IO, Task, Either, ZIO or a test effect, and the choice is made once at the edge of the application.
Tests replace the interpreter instead of the effect, so most specs need no mocking framework and no asynchronous runtime.
tradeoffs: Constraint creep ("MTL soup"): every capability a program uses becomes a type-class constraint on every function that needs it, so signatures grow until the program is polymorphic in nearly everything and abstract in nothing.

Dictionary indirection costs: the type-class call cannot be inlined, so a compiler cannot specialise the program for the concrete effect the way direct calls to IO would be; performance-critical paths end up using a concrete effect anyway.
Half of the expression problem remains: adding an *operation* still touches every interpreter, because all operations live in one algebra; only new interpreters are free.

No introspection: since there is no syntax tree, a program cannot be serialised, optimised, pattern-matched or sent over the wire - those needs force the initial encoding (or Boehm-Berarducci machinery) back in.

The meaning of a program is invisible locally: effect constraints are implicit at the call site, so a reader cannot see which effects a function performs without reading its constraint list, and law violations in a hand-written instance break the program silently.

Host-language tax: in languages without higher-kinded types the encoding has to be emulated (Kind wrappers, defunctionalisation, type erasure), and that machinery leaks into every signature it touches.

participants.responsibility: Declares the domain's constructs as operations over an opaque interpretation type; it carries the syntax of the embedded language and nothing about its meaning.
A value or function written only in terms of the algebra, polymorphic in the interpretation type; it composes operations and is instantiated by an interpreter at the edge of the application.
Supplies one concrete meaning for every operation of the algebra (evaluate, print, compile, record, mock); one instance per meaning, chosen where the program is run.

The type the algebra produces into - a plain type (Int, String, SQL query) or an effect type constructor (F[_] instantiated as IO, Task, Either, ZIO); it is what makes the same program reusable across effects.

The type-class instance supplying generic operations the program needs beyond its own algebra (Monad/Applicative for sequencing, Sync/Async for effectful primitives); passed as an implicit parameter or an explicit argument.

use_cases: A domain core (billing rules, order workflow, access rules) written once and run over the production effect in the application and over a pure test interpreter in the specs.
An embedded DSL whose single source is interpreted as evaluation, pretty-printing, SQL generation and cost analysis - for example a query or filter language.
A logging, metrics or clock capability behind an algebra, so tests record calls in memory instead of touching the real system, and production binds the real implementation at the edge.
Application ports in a hexagonal architecture where each port is a small algebra and adapters are the interpreters, keeping the effect type out of the core.

Compiler or pipeline front ends whose stages (parse, normalise, optimise, emit) are interpretations of one shared algebra rather than separate passes over a shared tree, including partial evaluation and staging.
Feature-flagged or multi-target output (HTML, PDF, JSON) produced by different interpreters of the same document algebra instead of branching inside the renderer.

A library ecosystem built on the encoding itself: Typelevel's cats-tagless derives FunctorK instances for tagless-final algebras so an interpreter written for F is lifted along a natural transformation F ~> G (e.g. Try into Free[Try, *] for stack safety) and composed horizontally with productK - machinery that has no counterpart for a concrete effect type.

A database DSL interpreted over two effect systems: epifab/cql4s defines one type-safe CQL algebra in Scala 3 and ships separate interpreter modules (cql4s-cats for Cats Effect/fs2, cql4s-zio for ZIO 2), so the same query program runs over whichever effect the application binds at its edge.

Haskell's mtl package is this encoding in production form: components are written once against monad classes (MonadReader, MonadState, MonadError or an application-defined class) over an abstract monad, and any transformer stack - or a hand-written instance over IO, or Identity for pure tests - serves as the interpreter.
avoid_when: The program must be inspected, serialised, optimised or sent over a network as data - choose the initial encoding (a tagged AST with an interpreter, i.e. interpreter-as-data) or a free monad instead.
There is exactly one interpretation and no test double is needed: plain functions or a direct call to the concrete effect are simpler than an algebra with a single instance.
The team has no type-class background and the codebase is small: ordinary dependency injection of an interface costs less to read and maintain.
The hot path cannot afford dictionary indirection (tight numeric loops, high-frequency trading, DSP): keep the algebra at the boundaries and the concrete effect or concrete types in the core.
Only one effect will ever be used and the language has no higher-kinded types - an interface with the concrete effect in its signatures gives the same structure with far less machinery.
The program is a one-off script: abstracting over an interpretation that will not change is pure overhead.
anti_patterns: "MTL soup": every function carries so many constraints that the program is polymorphic in everything and readable by no one - the abstraction has eaten its own benefit.

Naming the concrete effect inside the abstract program (calling IO/Future/Task directly, or demanding a lift-everything capability), which silently turns tagless final into a wrapper around one monad.
Interpreter bloat: moving domain decisions into the interpreter instead of the program, so each new interpretation must re-derive business rules and the interpreters disagree.
A tagless-final algebra in a codebase with a single interpreter and no tests to speak of - architecture theatre whose only effect is indirection.
Hand-written instances that violate the type-class laws (a Monad whose flatMap breaks associativity), which makes the program's behaviour depend on which interpreter happens to be in scope.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: the program depends on the algebra (an abstraction it owns), and the effect depends on it - the effect is the detail, not the program.
Open/closed principle, interpreter axis: adding a new interpretation must not modify a single program.
Information hiding: the interpretation type is opaque inside the program; nothing may assume it is Int, String or IO.
Interface segregation: many small algebras composed by constraints beat one wide interface, so interpreters implement only what they can honestly support.
Lawfulness: instances must satisfy the functor/monad/effect laws - the abstraction is sound only if its dictionaries are.
Composition over inheritance: capabilities are composed as parameters and constraints, never as a class hierarchy of interpreters.
best_practices: Write the program as a polymorphic value/function (one that names no concrete effect) and bind the effect exactly once, in the entry point.
Keep algebras small and orthogonal (console, clock, repository, logger) and compose them with constraints rather than accumulating operations in one interface.
Always ship at least two interpreters - the production one and an in-memory / recording one - so the abstraction is exercised and the tests stay pure.
Give the algebra no capability it does not need: if an operation requires Monad, say so at the algebra, not at every call site.
Keep the interpreters total: a missing operation must be a compile-time error, never a runtime surprise.
For performance-sensitive DSLs, add a staging or partial-evaluation interpreter (compile the program once) instead of giving up the encoding.
Test the laws of hand-written instances (functor/monad/effect laws) once, next to the instance.
Prefer the language's own realization of implicit resolution (type classes, given/implicit, traits) over hand-threaded dictionaries where the host has it.
sources: Carette, Kiselyov & Shan, Finally Tagless, Partially Evaluated: Tagless Staged Interpreters for Simpler Typed Languages, Journal of Functional Programming 19(5):509-543, 2009 - the first paper of the tagless-final family (the name itself stuck later).
Kiselyov, Typed Tagless Final Interpreters: The First, Introductory Course, in Generic and Indexed Programming (SSGIP 2010), LNCS 7470, Springer 2012, pp. 130-174 - the introductory lecture notes.

https://degoes.net/articles/tagless-horror - Rattray, 'The False Hope of Managing Effects with Tagless-Final in Scala': over-broad F constraints ("sync bloat") and lawless instances defeat the pattern's promised testability and reasoning benefits.
